#3486. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3484. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

Use this beginner-friendly plan to cut your risk of all-cause mortality by 45%

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It’s an age-old conundrum faced by beginners and experienced exercisers alike, assuming you can’t improve one without undermining the other.

But hybrid training, the increasingly popular practice of developing strength and fitness side-by-side, flips this principle on its head.

New research suggests doing both could even add years to your life.

According to an observational study following 147,000 health professionals over three decades, mortality risk was lowest among participants who trained cardio and strength.

Compared with doing neither, combining one to two hours of resistance training with a hearty dose of aerobic activity (30-45 MET-hours per week) reduced mortality risk by 45%.

For context, 30 Metabolic Equivalent of Task (MET) hours per week is roughly three times the minimum physical activity guidelines for Americans, equating to several hours of brisk walking, running or other moderate-to-vigorous activity.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Strength training alone was also associated with a strong reduction in all-cause mortality (13%). As was aerobic exercise. But combining both led to the greatest results.

That’s no surprise to Charlie Marchon, Co-Founder and Head of MARCHON Training, who specializes in the field of hybrid training and devised this accessible seven-day plan.

“At MARCHON, hybrid training means developing multiple performance qualities side-by-side. Put simply: strength and conditioning,” he tells Tom’s Guide.

“The science lies in managing the interference effect, so that strength and endurance training don't get in each other's way.”

That, he explains, comes down to how sessions are ordered, how hard each one is, and how much recovery sits between them. “At beginner level the interference effect is small and sensible amounts of each will improve both.”

Here, you’ll find Marchon’s seven-day hybrid training plan, plus advice on how to measure improvement and progress the plan over the course of six weeks.

Charlie Marchon is Co-Founder and Head of MARCHON Training, the training app built around structured, coach-designed programmes for strength, conditioning and hybrid racing. A Strength and Conditioning coach with 10 years of experience, he has programmed for everyone from complete beginners to competitive athletes.

How to use this hybrid training plan to build strength and cardio

To complete this plan, you’ll need two pairs of dumbbells—one lighter for pressing movements and one heavier for squats, hinges and rows.

The week is divided up into three types of sessions:

While suitable for beginners, exercising six days per week will be a big jump if coming from a standing start.

If you’re short on time or would rather ease in slowly, Marchon recommends stripping it back to just the Monday strength workout, Thursday intervals and Saturday hybrid circuit.

“That three-day version still covers strength, harder running and the hybrid link,” he says.

2B Dumbbell floor press (or bench press if available)

Take five to 10 minutes to warm up. Do a three-minute brisk walk or jog to raise your temperature, three minutes of bodyweight lunges, inchworms and glute bridges, then two lighter sets of your first superset before your first working set. For each superset, perform exercise A, rest for 30 seconds, then exercise B, rest for 60-90 seconds.

Marchon says: “A squat and a pull, then a hinge and a push. Every major muscle group gets worked without two exercises fighting for the same muscles back to back.”

20-40min run at an easy pace (3-4 out of 10 RPE)

Warm up with a brisk three-minute walk or easy jog. Swing your legs forward and back then side to side for 10 reps. Do 10 walking lunges, 20 small pogo hops on the balls of your feet, 20m of high knees and 20m of heel flicks. Then you’re good to go. Once complete, walk for five minutes then gently stretch your calves and hips.

Marchon says: “Easy running builds your aerobic base and lets you recover from Monday. The pace will feel slow. Don't try to chase intensity. Hold a conversational pace throughout, meaning you can speak in full sentences without pausing for breath. If you can’t run that long yet, alternate two minutes of running with one minute of walking.”

Warm up and cool down as per Monday’s strength workout. For each superset, perform exercise A, rest for 30 seconds, then perform exercise B, and rest for 60-90 seconds.

Marchon says: “This session swaps in single-leg and overhead work, so you're challenged in different positions to Monday.”

Warm up as per Tuesday’s run, finishing the 10min easy jog with three 10-second sprints to get ready for faster running. The intervals should feel comfortably hard, meaning you can utter a few words at a time, no more. Let your breathing settle during the two-minute recoveries before each next effort.

Marchon says: “The one harder run of the week. Short efforts improve your speed and your heart's capacity without the strain of a long hard run. Aim to run every effort at the same pace. If the last one is much slower than the first, you started too fast.”

Walking, mobility, or a gentle yoga class is fine, but keep it light.

Marchon says: “Recovery is where the adaptation happens, so take this day seriously.”

Warm up as per Tuesday’s run, then perform one easy practice round of the stations above with light dumbbells before you start. Aim to complete four rounds, resting one minute between rounds. Use moderate weights. This is about moving continuously, not lifting heavy.

Marchon says: “This hybrid session ties the week together. You run, then lift, then run again while you're still a little tired, which builds the ability to keep moving well under fatigue. Treadmill users can do the runs indoors. Outdoors, run an out and back route of 90 seconds each way and leave the dumbbells at your starting point.”

30-40min run at an easy pace (3-4/10 RPE)

Warm up and cool down as per Tuesday’s easy run. Set a pace that means you finish feeling like you could have gone further.

Marchon says: “This long easy run is optional in week one; it becomes a key session as the plan progresses. You can use run-walk intervals if you need. If your legs feel heavy from the week, swap in a brisk walk for 45 minutes.”

This week-long hybrid training plan sets the template to build both strength and cardio in parallel. Marchon recommends sticking with it for a minimum of six weeks.

“Think long term,” he says. “The real aim is a lasting training habit that keeps improving your strength, fitness, health and longevity.”

That means challenging yourself with slightly heavier weights, running for slightly longer, or repeating an extra few reps, sets, or intervals as your strength and fitness improves.

If your sleep starts to suffer, you still feel sore 48 hours after a session, or something hurts rather than just feels worked, Marchon suggests repeating the week rather than moving on.

“Progress that holds beats progress that breaks,” he says.

After six weeks, Marchon suggests repeating the six-week plan starting with your new weights and run times.

“Minimal kit will take you a long way, but in time you'll need heavier weights and more structured training to keep challenging yourself.”

#3482. One of the Best QLED TVs of 2026 Is Over $1,300 Off Right Now

TCL has been pushing the boundaries of QLED TVs, making some of the best in the market at very competitive prices. This year, the company released its QM8L model, introducing a new design and impressive features and specs to a series that isn't even their flagship. Right now, the 65-inch QM8L is $1,197.99 (originally $2,499.99), $100 cheaper than it was just earlier this month, reaching its lowest price since it launched in April, according to price-tracking tools. Larger sizes are also seeing substantial discounts.

One of the first things you'll notice about the QM8L is the “Zero Border” bezel design, which gives it a modern, minimalistic look. When you turn it on, you'll likely note how bright this TV gets, which is a huge advantage QLEDs have over OLEDs. TCL claims it reaches 6,000 nits—seeing as the brightest OLED TV on the market only reaches 700 nits, no OLED can come close to this unit's brightness. Another important spec to note here is the local dimming zones: TCL claims this TV has up to 4,000, which means it gets top-tier backlight control, limited light blooming (thanks in part to TCL's "Halo Control"), and incredible contrast levels that some might not be able to distinguish from an OLED.

As many of us won't manually calibrate our TVs, the picture modes you can switch to in the settings will be most people's go-to. This TV's "Filmmaker mode" provides accurate color and picture, and if you're a gamer, you can use the native 144Hz high-refresh rate. If you don't already have a surround sound system at home and want to keep a minimalist setup, the QM8L comes with Dolby Atmos-ready Bang & Olufsen speakers, which offer above-average audio output compared to most TVs. You can read more about these features in CNET's 8.8/10 review. If 65 inches isn't quite right for your home theater setup, take a look at the QM8L's other sizes, which are also discounted right now.

#3481. All 6 Episodes Of Paramount+'s Action Series Deliver Video Game Fun At Its Best

One of the best miniseries to come out of Paramount+ is a surprisingly entertaining video game adapted series that deserves more love. Paramount+ as a platform has become an incredible hub for interesting action stories, from the Yellowstone universe built brick by brick thanks to Taylor Sheridan, to the Dexter saga of shows about a killer with a code, there is a lot to uncover.

However, one of the most fascinating shows on the platform takes a very different approach to storytelling, which may in part be down to the fact that it depicts a character from a video game series. Of course, the show is Knuckles, the spin-off limited series from the popular Sonic movies, starring Idris Elba as the titular echidna.

And while the show shifts the focus from the blue hedgehog, the series manages to create a thoroughly fun and inventive six episodes that contain the energy of a video game while also building out the world of the films in a way that makes some of the supporting characters a much larger part of the narrative.

It's fair to say that the expectations around the Knuckles series were not particularly high before the show came out. As much as Elba is a massive Hollywood star, and the opportunity to see him expand his character was enticing, Knuckles was clearly changing course from the epic adventures depicted in the films.

That being said, this did open the door to make this series a fun, low-stakes entry in the franchise that could feel like side quests in a video game, and take the audience on a journey that fleshes out a less pivotal part of the story as a way of becoming more immersed and getting closer to other characters who rarely got a chance to shine.

With that in mind, Knuckles is a wonderful addition to the live-action Sonic saga, which also places Adam Pally's Wade Whipple into a central role as he teams up with Knuckles to train for a bowling tournament. There are also surprisingly competent and compelling action sequences when Knuckles faces off against enemies, and visual effects that rival the big-budget movies.

For the longest time, video game adaptations proved to be the bane of Hollywood. Despite being rich source material for adapting big stories, with built-in fanbases who were thoroughly invested in the narrative, most movies and shows depicting the world of video games fell far short of the quality familiar audiences expected, and they ultimately failed to capture the characters and emotions of the stories they were trying to adapt.

Thankfully, 2020s Sonic the Hedgehog was among the first films to shake off the curse of bad video game adaptations thanks to the incredible casting, the willingness to lean into goofy and absurd humor, and the clear elements of the game that were successfully brought to the big screen, such as Jim Carrey's Dr. Robotnik, the connection to golden rings, and Sonic's signature sense of humor and appetite.

Knuckles built on that foundation with a series that accurately adapts a more sullen character, while also creating a competent narrative where he engages in a task that seems outrageous, and then layers in some action and intensity for balance. It's a wonderful entry that deserves more attention and love for the way it navigates a story that could have fallen flat.

Of course, there are some divided opinions regarding the series, but that is true for every film in the Sonic franchise as well. What is certain is that this series is in-keeping with the wider saga, and it manages to overcome so many of the challenges that have plagued video game adaptations for decades. Knuckles sticks the landing, and it's a great addition to an already great franchise.

#3480. Tom Hiddleston's Near-Perfect Apple TV Miniseries Gets Better With Every Episode

Period dramas span a wide range of shows, including everything from romances to war stories. This variety gives fans almost too many options to watch, and though several have become well known, others inevitably fly under the radar. One such example is Apple TV's The Essex Serpent. The 2022 miniseries is an unpredictable entry in the genre, but even four years out from its release, it's one that period drama fans shouldn't miss.

Adapted from Sarah Perry's novel of the same name, the Apple TV miniseries stars Claire Danes and Tom Hiddleston, whose performances set the show apart. Beyond its recognizable leading duo, the series distinguishes itself with a slowly building tension as the story unfolds and shifts, making it impossible to stop watching. Consisting of just six episodes, The Essex Serpent is an easy binge for genre fans that will not disappoint.

The Essex Serpent is a Victorian-era gothic romance centered around Cora Seaborne (Danes), a newly widowed woman and a paleontology enthusiast. Rather than mourning the death of her abusive husband, Cora uses her newfound freedom to indulge her scientific interests by investigating reports of the Essex Serpent, a mythical creature said to be preying on the village of Aldwinter. Packing up her son, Frankie (Michael Jibson), and her companion, Martha (Hayley Squires), Cora travels to Aldwinter to see what she can uncover.

There can never be too many period dramas.

Once in Aldwinter, Cora learns that the residents fully believe the creature is responsible for local tragedies — except for the village's skeptical vicar, Will (Hiddleston), who forges an intellectual bond with Cora. The possibility of anything more is risky, considering Will is already married to Stella (Clémence Poésy), yet the love triangle that forms between them holds its own surprises. As locals disappear and disaster mounts, the villagers grow suspicious of Cora despite her attempts to help. Rather than the creature story it initially seems to be, The Essex Serpent focuses on deeper themes to create a character-driven narrative with slowly building tension.

The Essex Serpent's main narrative obstacle isn't the potential existence of the titular creature itself, but the dangerous hysteria in Aldwinter as well as the complicated romance between Cora and Will, both of which take time to build. Ultimately, the characters are the story's greatest strength, with the series relying on their complex emotional journeys to carry the show. Thanks to the talented cast, especially standouts Danes and Hiddleston, the miniseries explores layered people that make The Essex Serpent a rewarding watch.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

While there's plenty to set The Essex Serpent apart, Danes' character is a highlight. Subverting the expectations of a traditional Victorian heroine, Cora's deep belief in science and natural skepticism make her compelling to watch. Additionally, the story makes no secret of her abusive marriage, but allows her to escape following her husband's death and pursue her own intellectual interests. The Essex Serpent may have been overlooked, but it isn't lacking in surprising twists and turns, and its short format rewards any period drama fan looking for a thrilling weekend binge.

The Steam Deck is one of the best purchases I’ve ever made. Valve’s handheld PC can play so many games with ease. However, with the Steam Machine and Steam Frame now available, the Steam Deck is still one of the best handhelds for retro gaming in 2026.

I’ve always been a retro gamer. I grew up with Sonic the Hedgehog, Tomb Raider, Metal Gear Solid, and others. I’ve carried a PS Vita in my backpack for years so I could play titles from each of these series, and more, on the go. Granted, recent remasters mean I haven’t needed to use the Vita as much, but plenty still hasn't appeared on modern systems.

It’s why the Steam Deck fills that gap. Not only can I play DRM-free games via GOG and many Steam games that haven't been updated in years, but I can also use many emulators, giving me access to titles that have next to no chance of appearing anytime soon. With that in mind, here’s how you can set up your Steam Deck as a powerful retro handheld.

Although the Steam Deck OLED is almost 3 years old as of this writing, it’s still powerful enough to play plenty of games from the PlayStation 3 era. Games like Star Wars: Rogue Squadron II and Dead or Alive 3 run at full speed thanks to Dolphin and Xemu, respectively.

But setting up all these emulators can be a hassle, which is where EmuDeck comes in. In less than 10 minutes, you can transfer games from your PC or Mac to your Steam Deck via its ROM Manager, and start playing games from your childhood. Better yet, EmuDeck works with SteamOS, so any titles you transfer will sit alongside your Steam library.

You don’t have to install every emulator, perhaps a few, just to save space on your Steam Deck. EmuDeck gives you plenty of control over your games and BIOS files, as well as how they look on the handheld’s display. The app is a fantastic way of playing games from your past without much hassle.

If you own a Steam Deck but have been tempted to play The Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker HD or Tekken Tag Tournament, EmuDeck will make it happen. But something else has been making the Steam Deck an essential retro gaming machine that doesn’t run via emulators.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

2026 will be known as the year when decompilations exploded, and for good reason. For anyone unaware, decompilations reverse-engineer games into source code, meaning long-standing bugs can be fixed and new features can be added. For example, Harbour Masters has released decompilations of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Banjo-Kazooie, Star Fox 64, and more.

You can play these on the best Windows PCs or Macs in native widescreen, with quality-of-life features and more benefits. But you can play plenty of others right now. The decomps subreddit mostly keeps track of what’s in development - with many of them not made by AI.

Wes Fenlon has a fantastic, frequently updated overview of decompilations and recompilations of classic games, and it also means many of these re-releases can be played on Steam Deck. Many, like Harbour Masters, offer a Linux version, so it’s a matter of installing the file and following a few steps to get it up and running.

It’s another way to preserve certain games that run even better than emulation. It’s also better for battery life on the Steam Deck, since these are native ports, meaning the CPU and GPU use less power to run the game. When you consider the native display resolution and graphical settings for these decompilations, it makes these games feel like they were meant to be played this way on the Steam Deck.

Game preservation is in a state of interesting flux. Emulators are now running games as originally intended, with no major graphical glitches or slowdown on devices from the Raspberry Pi to the Steam Deck. New emulators for PS4 and PS5 are already beginning to appear, which means games like Astro Bot and Marvel's Wolverine could someday be playable on a future Steam Deck handheld.

But there’s also the matter of decompilations. Plenty of AI-vibe-coded ones have recently appeared, to the detriment of others that have passionately reverse-engineered classic games with care and determination. You can keep track of others that are close to being fully decompiled at decomp.dev, with titles like Silent Hill, Starfox Adventures, and Super Smash Bros. Melee that could have the same benefits as Harbour Masters’ The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time decompilation someday.

Nevertheless, this is all good news for your Steam Deck. Emulation and decompilations give your handheld another way to play your favorite games on the go, including eras like the Game Boy and PlayStation 3. As things stand, it looks like there are plenty more decompiled titles to look forward to playing on it.

#3477. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

The winter air-drying rules that actually cut your laundry drying time in half

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When cold, wet weather rolls in, drying laundry indoors without a clothes dryer often turns into a multi-day ordeal. Piles of damp fabric draped across clothes airers bring chilling humidity into your living space, leaving garments smelling stale and walls prone to condensation and mould.

The secret to slashing indoor drying times lies not in cranking up the central heating to full blast, but in mastering air movement, extraction, and strategic placement. Here is how to dry your clothes indoors quickly and cleanly this winter, without inviting damp, mold, or musty smells into your home.

The single most effective shortcut begins before your clothes even leave the washing machine drum. Most spin cycles leave substantial moisture trapped deep inside thick cottons, heavy jeans, and knitwear.

Running a dedicated second spin cycle at your machine’s maximum spin speed pulls out surprising amounts of excess water without adding heat or risking fabric damage.

Shaking each item out vigorously immediately after unloading loosens compacted fibres and opens up airflow pockets that otherwise trap dampness for hours.

Where and how you hang wet laundry makes the difference between fresh clothes in hours and musty garments after two days. Cramming items closely onto a clothes drying rack restricts air circulation, trapping damp air directly between layers of fabric.

If you can, space each garment across two rungs rather than one, or slip button-up shirts and tops onto sturdy coat hangers suspended along the outer frame to keep fabrics exposed to circulating room air.

Moisture evaporates only as fast as the surrounding air can absorb and carry it away. Trapping a full airer in a closed, cold room creates a humid microclimate that halts evaporation entirely.

Positioning your clothes airer roughly a foot away from a heating duct, never draped directly in front of it, which blocks heating efficiency and risks scorching fabrics, paired with an oscillating fan on its lowest setting forces air constantly across the textiles.

If your home struggles with persistent condensation in late fall and winter, running one of the best dehumidifiers directly beneath or alongside the rack draws pints of moisture straight out of the wet fibres while blowing warm, dry air back through the load.

#3474. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3473. The Sci-Fi Masterpiece That Ridley Scott Dismissed as Too “Slow” Is Officially Streaming for Free

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

Director Ridley Scott made a disappointing return to the sci-fi genre this year, with the post-apocalyptic movie The Dog Stars. Starring Jacob Elordi in the lead role, the film grossed around $40 million worldwide against a reported budget of approximately $100 million. Around the same time as the film's release and mediocre reception, Scott announced his intention to return to the Alien franchise, which he helped create in the 1970s. The only trouble is that the franchise was going in an entirely different direction, one that Scott clearly wasn't too impressed by. Scott voiced similar reservations about another reboot of one of his most memorable movies. The movie in question was recently added to a free streaming platform.

A couple of years ago, director Fede Álvarez successfully rebooted the Alien series with Alien: Romulus, which grossed $350 million worldwide against a reported budget of $80 million, and received excellent reviews. A sequel to the movie was quickly announced, but some time later, Álvarez revealed that he wouldn't be returning as director. Scott said in an interview that he found the movie to be just "okay," and that he intends to revisit the narrative that he began with Prometheus and Alien: Covenant.

While Prometheus grossed more than $400 million worldwide, Covenant underperformed with around $240 million globally and brought the franchise to a halt. It wasn't until Romulus that the series appeared to have been resurrected. However, with Scott effectively wanting to erase the movie entirely, it remains to be seen where the series will go next. Curiously, Scott made similar comments about Denis Villeneuve's Blade Runner 2049.

Released in 2017, the legacy sequel received phenomenal reviews but underperformed commercially. It ended up grossing only around $280 million worldwide against a reported budget of more than $180 million. However, many found it to be an improvement over Scott's original, the classic sci-fi noir Blade Runner. Scott disagreed with this contingent, saying in an interview that he found Blade Runner 2049 to be too "slow" and too "long."

The movie now holds a "Certified Fresh" 88% score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, where the consensus reads, "Visually stunning and narratively satisfying, Blade Runner 2049 deepens and expands its predecessor's story while standing as an impressive filmmaking achievement in its own right." The Blade Runner franchise will be rebooted on November 25 with the Prime Video series Blade Runner 2099, starring Hunter Schafer and Michelle Yeoh. Meanwhile, you can revisit Villeneuve's epic on Pluto TV.

#3472. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

#3471. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

#3469. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

JBL’s Live 780NC over-ear headphones are down to $139.95 from $249.95, a $110 discount that brings them to their lowest price ever, according to price trackers. They’re designed for people who like to wear headphones for hours at a time, too, with adjustable metal sliders and earcups that pivot to fit comfortably around your head. The earcups also fold flat to make them easier to pack, although the included soft pouch offers less protection in a bag than a hard case would.

Del Casher -- the inventor of the wah-wah pedal, renowned guitarist, and film and TV composer -- has died ... TMZ has learned.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

Have you recently checked out a certain Irishman's latest action-thriller involving a combat veteran? Then you’re likely keen to revisit some of Liam Neeson’s past action work. I’ve got you covered on that front. Cold, charismatic and with an iconic accent that could melt steel, how can you not love this actor’s stellar CV?

I’ve adored Liam ever since I first saw him in 1995’s “Rob Roy”, even if his Highland accent isn’t the best. Hey, I’m Scottish (I can judge). Over the last 20 years of tackling terrorists and timber wolves, Neeson has become a slightly unlikely action star. After all, how many performers can claim to be an actual Jedi who has also starred in a Steven Spielberg Best Picture winner? ‘One’ is the answer. His name is Liam Neeson, and here are three action movies you need to watch after seeing “The Mongoose”.

Ah yes, the film that alerted the world to Mr. Nesson’s “very particular set of skills”. Said skills happen to include beating bad guys rotten, should they be silly enough to kidnap Big Liam’s daughter. Though it seems bizarre to say, considering he played the main role in 1993’s widely acclaimed “Schindler’s List”, 2008’s “Taken” does feel like the iconic North Irishman’s most pivotal part.

However “The Mongoose” ultimately performs at the box office, you could argue the main reason Neeson’s latest project exists is because of “Taken”. In playing a vengeful father capable of kicking serious ass well into middle age, Liam laid down the blueprint for 20 years’ worth of solid action work. This thriller pinned Neeson as the go-to hard guy with a heart. He’s deservedly lived well off that image ever since.

Watch "Taken" on Prime Video (buy/rent) now

Let me paint you a picture: Liam Neeson vs wolves. That’s it. You’re either in or you’re out… and you should definitely be in. The premise is semi-absurd — Neeson’s refinery worker survives a plane crash in Alaska then has to beat up fluffy timber predators — but “The Grey” totally works as a no-frills ‘guilty pleasure’ movie. Don’t let anyone ever judge you for enjoying Liam kicking CGI wolves to the turf.

Admittedly, said effects haven’t aged that well. Hollywood continues to have a problem nailing down convincing CG fur. Still, that shouldn't put you off this chilly thriller. The whole reason the movie works is because Neeson treats proceedings with his trademark sense of unironic gravitas. When he kicks a computer-generated canine in the face, you know he believes it. After the all-timer that is 1981’s “American Werewolf in London”, this is definitely my second favorite lupine flick.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Watch "The Grey on Prime Video (buy/rent) now

The Year of our Lord 2011 was a big one for Mr. Neeson. Qui-Gon Jinn really enjoyed getting into crashes over this 12 month period (see “The Grey” above). A handsome man who is at least six feet and four inches tall shouldn’t be able to play a low-key doctor so well, but that’s Jedi mind tricks for you. Hollywood has seen Neeson as an every man for a couple of decades now, even in real life you know the actor could slay you with an upper eyebrow.

A Berlin-set tale of stolen identities, there’s a hint of Hitchcock classic “North by Northwest” about this Neeson thriller; even if the film takes itself more seriously than Alfred’s iconic dark comedy. The convenient "Amnesia Effect” trope is admittedly on the nose, but Neeson plays out the action with his typified class. It’s no "Schindler's List”, but "Unknown" is still worth 113 minutes of your time.

#3462. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3461. Justin Timberlake Reveals Britney Spears Did Not Inspire 'What Goes Around… Comes Around'

Justin Timberlake is dispelling a longstanding rumor about the origins of one of his hit songs ... and apparently it was never about Britney Spears.

Speaking with Complex's "Re-Rank" show ... JT said the song "What Goes Around... Comes Around" was "actually a personal story from a friend's" that he got permission to use.

He added ... "He was just going through it, and he was telling me what had happened, and said, 'Do you mind if I write about this?' And I quote, my friend said, 'Yeah, torch that bitch. What goes around comes around.' And I was like, 'I have to go, thank you.' He was like, 'What?' I was like, ‘I got it.’"

After hanging up the phone with his pal ... Justin said it took only 20 minutes to write the hit.

The 2006 hit came with much speculation that it was about JT's ex Britney Spears ... including rumors that it was a follow-up to his 2002 banger "Cry Me a River."

Now "Cry Me a River" may be a different matter ... as Justin hasn't said one way or another if Britney inspired it or not.

Without naming her ... Justin wrote in his 2018 book "Hindsight: & All the Things I Can't See in Front of Me" about the songwriting process ... "I've been scorned. I've been pissed off. I wrote 'Cry Me a River' in two hours. I didn't plan on writing it."

Hopefully we'll get more insight with Justin's upcoming docuseries.
